# How Should You Write Cold Email to Dental Practices?


[Griffin Morris](https://re2.ai/authors/griffin-morris) ·


October 12, 2026


·


3 min read


If we were building a cold-outreach campaign to dental practices, we would write the first message for someone responsible for the practice's results.


That means leading with a concrete outcome, such as financing another operatory or booking more implant consultations. We would not default to language about company-wide programs, vendor consolidation or rollout across offices.


The reason is simple: dental practices are more independent than any other local-business category we measured.


## Dental practices stand apart from other local businesses


Resquared's October 2026 Main Street Index included 14,786,458 businesses marked active in the US and Canada.


Among the 282,430 dental practices in that group, 96% were independent. In this case, independent means the practice was not part of a multi-location brand. Across all businesses in the Index, 87% were independent.


So dental practices were 9 percentage points more likely than the average business to be independent. They also had the highest independent share among the eight categories in the Index.


That does not mean the owner personally reads every email. A practice may still have an office manager, gatekeeper or its own process for reviewing vendors.


It does mean your opening message should make sense at the practice level.


## What owner-level language sounds like


Owner-level language connects your offer to a recognizable financial or operating result.


For a lender, that might be purchasing imaging equipment, adding an operatory or managing cash during an expansion. For an agency, it might be filling appointment openings or generating demand for a specific service.


A lender could write:


> Are equipment costs delaying plans for another operatory? We help dental practices finance new equipment while preserving cash for the rest of the business. Would it be useful if I sent over a few examples?


The recipient can quickly understand what is being offered and why it might matter. If someone else handles financing, the message is also easy to route to that person.


Compare that with: "We provide flexible capital solutions for dental organizations."


The broader version sounds polished, but it makes the reader do the work. They have to figure out what the money is for, which problem it solves and whether it applies to their practice.


You do not need to mention ownership in the email. "Are you the owner?" is usually less useful than naming the problem your offer solves.


If your draft says "capital solutions," say what the capital helps the practice buy. If it says "growth strategy," name the service for which the practice wants more appointments.


## Separate practices from larger dental brands


A practice that belongs to a multi-location brand may have a central team reviewing lenders, agencies and other vendors. That group may care about consistency across locations, approval from headquarters or a broader rollout.


It should receive a different message.


Before starting outreach, divide the list into independent practices and practices connected to multi-location brands. For independent practices, lead with a result the practice can see. For larger brands, write for the team coordinating decisions across offices.


You can research this manually by checking each website for a locations page, shared branding or a parent organization. Or use Resquared, which already distinguishes independent local businesses from businesses connected to multi-location brands.


Do not combine both groups and smooth the email into language broad enough to fit either one. That is how you end up with phrases such as "integrated solutions for dental organizations" instead of a clear reason to reply.


## Treat this as the first test


The data tells you where to start. It does not tell you that every dental campaign should use identical copy.


Keep the audience and offer consistent, then test the framing. A lender might compare a message about financing equipment with one about preserving cash during expansion. An agency might compare a general patient-growth message with one focused on implant consultations.


Judge the versions by which one starts more real conversations with the dental practices you want to reach. Your offer may perform best with language that breaks a common cold-email best practice. That is fine. Start with what the market structure suggests, then let replies tell you what to change.


For the first version, name one result that matters inside the practice and make that result the reason to respond.
